ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants were presented with auditory sentences that contained a highly predictable word, such as cloud in The tourists expected rain when the sun went behind the cloud.
table.header: Study 2: Estimating and comparing divergences between conditions

table.text: The sequential analysis showed that participants were more likely to look at the target object than at the unrelated object starting 400 ms after display onset.
table.header: Study 2: Estimating and comparing divergences between conditions

table.text: In addition, participants were more likely to look at the English competitor than at the unrelated object, but this effect was limited to a narrower time window between 500 and 650 ms.
table.header: Study 2: Estimating and comparing divergences between conditions

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants were presented with auditory sentences that contained a highly predictable word, such as cloud in The tourists expected rain when the sun went behind the cloud.

> The sequential analysis showed that participants were more likely to look at the target object than at the unrelated object starting 400 ms after display onset.

> In addition, participants were more likely to look at the English competitor than at the unrelated object, but this effect was limited to a narrower time window between 500 and 650 ms.

Dashed lines indicate 80% power and the nominal 5% Type I error rate."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 44 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were presented with auditory sentences that contained a highly predictable word, such as cloud in The tourists expected rain when the sun went behind the cloud.
The sequential analysis showed that participants were more likely to look at the target object than at the unrelated object starting 400 ms after display onset.
In addition, participants were more likely to look at the English competitor than at the unrelated object, but this effect was limited to a narrower time window between 500 and 650 ms.

info.title: D R A F T A novel method for detecting the onset of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking

author.affiliation:
School of Arts and Humanities
								University of Lisbon

text.text: Determining the onset of experimental effects in timeseries data is central to psycholinguistics, because onset timing constrains theories about when different types of linguistic information become available during language processing.
Several onset detection methods have been proposed for the visual world paradigm.
An increasingly adopted approach is the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021), but its accuracy in recovering underlying onset values has not yet been formally evaluated.
We address this gap with two simulation studies and propose a novel onset detection method based on generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) and posterior simulation.
This method integrates timecourse modelling with onset estimation and supports the direct comparison of onset times across experimental conditions and participant groups.
Our simulations showed that the GAMMbased method produced less biased and more accurate onset estimates than the bootstrap-based method, as well as generally better confidence interval coverage.
Although both methods tended to estimate onsets later than their underlying values, the delays were smaller for the GAMM-based method.
Differences in curve steepness could also produce spurious significant differences between estimated onsets, but these occurred less frequently with the GAMM-based method.
We demonstrate the practical application of the GAMM-based method by reanalysing two published visual world datasets and provide a user-friendly R package to facilitate its adoption.
By enabling more accurate estimation of effect timing in the visual world paradigm, our method can contribute to advancing theories of prediction and language comprehension.
We thank Aine Ito and Kate Stone for kindly providing access to their data.

We are also grateful to Shravan Vasishth, Dario Paape, and Titus von der Malsburg for helpful feedback on earlier versions of this work, and to Aine Ito and Bob McMurray for their constructive reviews.
A central goal of psycholinguistic research is to understand how language processing unfolds over time.
This often requires characterising the timecourse of experimental effects, including estimating the time points at which those effects first emerge-that is, their onsets.
Analyses of onset times can thus be instrumental for evaluating cognitive theories.

For example, the timecourse and ordering of semantic versus morphosyntactic processes are crucial points of debate for models of sentence processing (Friederici & Weissenborn, 2007; Reichle, 2021; Staub, 2015; Sturt, 2003) and visual word recognition (e.g., Feldman et al., 2009; Rastle & Davis, 2008).
text.formatted: For example, the timecourse and ordering of semantic versus morphosyntactic processes are crucial points of debate for models of sentence processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Friederici & Weissenborn, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Reichle, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Staub, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Sturt, 2003)</ref> and visual word recognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Feldman et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rastle & Davis, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Onset analyses are also relevant because the definition of some cognitive processes incorporates a temporal aspect that requires empirical evaluation.
For instance, predictive processes are often defined as the preactivation of input prior to it being seen or heard (Huettig et al., 2022; Pickering & Gambi, 2018; Schlenter, 2023).
text.formatted: For instance, predictive processes are often defined as the preactivation of input prior to it being seen or heard <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Huettig et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Pickering & Gambi, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Schlenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, assessing the onset of effects is relevant for theories that characterise specific populations in terms of their speed, which are often evaluated by quantifying temporal differences between participant groups.

Prominent examples include theories that predict processing delays in second language learners (Hopp, 2021; McDonald, 2006), ageing populations (Salthouse, 1996), and speakers with different types of language disorder (Haarmann & Kolk, 1991; Hanne et al., 2011; McMurray et al., 2022; Meyer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Prominent examples include theories that predict processing delays in second language learners <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hopp, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">McDonald, 2006)</ref>, ageing populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Salthouse, 1996)</ref>, and speakers with different types of language disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Haarmann & Kolk, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hanne et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">McMurray et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Meyer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A popular paradigm for assessing real-time language processing is visual world eyetracking (Magnuson, 2019; Tanenhaus et al., 1995).
text.formatted: A popular paradigm for assessing real-time language processing is visual world eyetracking <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Magnuson, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Tanenhaus et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: In the visual world paradigm, eye movements are recorded as people listen to spoken language while viewing objects or scenes.
The temporal sequence of eye movements is taken to reflect the evaluation of competing interpretations.
The core assumption is that when participants look more at one object than another, they are considering that object as the relevant referent at the time point of measurement.
A key advantage of the visual world paradigm is therefore its temporal resolution, that is, its ability to reveal how cognitive processes unfold over time.
Below, we review how different analytical approaches have leveraged this temporal resolution.

We provide examples of onset detection methods within each approach to illustrate their similarities and differences, and to situate the method proposed in this paper (for more extensive overviews, see Ito & Knoeferle, 2023; McMurray, 2023).
text.formatted: We provide examples of onset detection methods within each approach to illustrate their similarities and differences, and to situate the method proposed in this paper (for more extensive overviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ito & Knoeferle, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">McMurray, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Early analytical approaches to visual world data-which were historically related to eye-tracking during reading-focused on quantifying properties of oculomotor events such as fixations and saccades.

For example, they involved comparisons of the number of fixations to a specific image, their duration, and/or the probability of launching a saccade (McMurray, Clayards, et al., 2008; McMurray et al., 2009; Spivey & Marian, 1999; Tanenhaus et al., 1995).
text.formatted: For example, they involved comparisons of the number of fixations to a specific image, their duration, and/or the probability of launching a saccade <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(McMurray, Clayards, et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">McMurray et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Spivey & Marian, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Tanenhaus et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: These approaches are advantageous because they rely on physiologically grounded measures, but their use in the analysis of visual world data remains challenging.
One hurdle is the existence of multiple fixation measures.
For example, a particular cognitive process may simultaneously affect the number of fixations to an image, change their duration, and/or influence the probability of re-fixation.

Reading research tackled this issue by advancing hypotheses and computational models that link specific cognitive processes (e.g., retrieval interference) to specific reading measures (for review, see Schotter & Dillon, 2025).
text.formatted: Reading research tackled this issue by advancing hypotheses and computational models that link specific cognitive processes (e.g., retrieval interference) to specific reading measures (for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Schotter & Dillon, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: But in contrast to reading-a routinised and highly practised skill-the link between fixation measures and cognitive processes is less well-established in the visual world paradigm.

This is because eye movements in the visual world paradigm reflect multiple processes, including object recognition, lexical activation, and the mapping between linguistic and visual representations (Magnuson, 2019).
text.formatted: This is because eye movements in the visual world paradigm reflect multiple processes, including object recognition, lexical activation, and the mapping between linguistic and visual representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Magnuson, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, the space of potential measures expands, and there is currently no single obvious choice among them.

Moreover, the effect of any given cognitive process may be distributed across different measures, so a single measure may not contain a strong enough signal to be detected reliably, reducing statistical power (McMurray et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, the effect of any given cognitive process may be distributed across different measures, so a single measure may not contain a strong enough signal to be detected reliably, reducing statistical power <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(McMurray et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: An example of an onset detection method applied to oculomotor events can be found in Altmann (2011) and Salverda et al. (2014), who used the latency of the first saccade towards a target object to estimate the earliest time point at which information from the speech signal influenced eye movements.
text.formatted: An example of an onset detection method applied to oculomotor events can be found in <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Altmann (2011)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Salverda et al. (2014)</ref>, who used the latency of the first saccade towards a target object to estimate the earliest time point at which information from the speech signal influenced eye movements.

text.text: This approach has not been widely adopted, likely because it entails substantial data loss and comes with modelling limitations.

For instance, it requires removing a large proportion of trials (over 50% in Salverda et al., 2014), and was originally implemented using statistical tests that do not account for between-participant variability (for discussion, see Salverda et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For instance, it requires removing a large proportion of trials (over 50% in <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Salverda et al., 2014)</ref>, and was originally implemented using statistical tests that do not account for between-participant variability (for discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Salverda et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Partly because of the issues above, current analytical approaches in the visual world paradigm rarely operate directly on oculomotor events.
Instead, they rely on summaries of gaze behaviour over time, typically the proportion of looks directed to a given image at each time point.
The resulting timeseries are widely referred to as "fixation curves", despite being derived from gaze samples rather than discrete fixation events (McMurray, 2023).
text.formatted: The resulting timeseries are widely referred to as "fixation curves", despite being derived from gaze samples rather than discrete fixation events <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(McMurray, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Fixation curves are taken to reflect the timecourse of linguistic processing, an assumption supported by studies showing a close correspondence between these curves and the timecourse predictions from computational models of word recognition (Allopenna et al., 1998; Dahan et al., 2001; Hannagan et al., 2013; McClelland & Elman, 1986; McMurray et al., 2009 McMurray et al., , 2010;; Mirman et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Fixation curves are taken to reflect the timecourse of linguistic processing, an assumption supported by studies showing a close correspondence between these curves and the timecourse predictions from computational models of word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allopenna et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Dahan et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hannagan et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">McClelland & Elman, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">McMurray et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">McMurray et al., , 2010;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Mirman et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, fixation curves address some of the challenges of event-based measures by collapsing information from different properties (e.g., fixation probability and duration) into a single time-varying measure, reducing the number of dependent variables.
In addition, fixation curves can offer finer temporal specificity than event-based measures because they do not depend on identifying when individual fixations start or end (McMurray, 2023).
text.formatted: In addition, fixation curves can offer finer temporal specificity than event-based measures because they do not depend on identifying when individual fixations start or end <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(McMurray, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Approaches that rely on fixation curves can be divided into two types.
The first type comprises curve-fitting methods that focus on characterising the shape of the entire curve over time.

Prominent examples include growth-curve models (Mirman, 2014; Porretta et al., 2018), generalised additive mixed-effects models (GAMMs, Miwa & Baayen, 2021; Van Rij et al., 2016 , 2019), and bootstrapped differences of time series (BDOTS, Seedorff et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Prominent examples include growth-curve models <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Mirman, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Porretta et al., 2018)</ref>, generalised additive mixed-effects models <ref type="bibr">(GAMMs, Miwa & Baayen, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Van Rij et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">, 2019)</ref>, and bootstrapped differences of time series <ref type="bibr">(BDOTS, Seedorff et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These methods are model-based in the sense that they involve fitting explicit statistical models to the data, allowing researchers to estimate the full timecourse of looking preferences and to test whether these trajectories differ between conditions and/or participant groups.
A second type of method based on fixation curves can be called "index-based" (McMurray, 2023).
text.formatted: A second type of method based on fixation curves can be called "index-based" <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(McMurray, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These methods use fixation curves as a starting point, but instead of modelling their full trajectory, they derive indices that summarise specific properties of the curve.
Some indices capture the magnitude of looking preferences, such as the average proportion of target looks within a time window of interest.
Other indices capture timing properties, such as the time point at which looks to the competitor reach their peak proportion (McMurray et al., 2010; Rigler et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Other indices capture timing properties, such as the time point at which looks to the competitor reach their peak proportion <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(McMurray et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Rigler et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Within index-based approaches, onsets (i.e., when an effect first emerges) are likewise timing indices.
A number of procedures have been proposed to estimate onset times from fixation curves.
One approach is to conduct sequential statistical tests at each time bin to determine the earliest time point at which an effect is significantly detected (Ben-David et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2018).
text.formatted: One approach is to conduct sequential statistical tests at each time bin to determine the earliest time point at which an effect is significantly detected <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ben-David et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ito et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although this method yields an onset estimate for a given effect of interest, it does not provide a measure of temporal uncertainty around the onset and does not allow comparisons of onset times between conditions or groups (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021).
text.formatted: Although this method yields an onset estimate for a given effect of interest, it does not provide a measure of temporal uncertainty around the onset and does not allow comparisons of onset times between conditions or groups <ref type="bibr">(Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Another method, which was borrowed from the ERP literature (J. Miller et al., 1998; Ulrich & Miller, 2001), defines an onset as the first time point at which a measure or effect exceeds a fixed percentage of its maximum (e.g., 50%) and then uses jackknifing to derive participant-level estimates that can be submitted to standard statistical tests (Galle et al., 2019; McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013).
text.formatted: Another method, which was borrowed from the ERP literature (J. <ref type="bibr">Miller et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ulrich & Miller, 2001)</ref>, defines an onset as the first time point at which a measure or effect exceeds a fixed percentage of its maximum (e.g., 50%) and then uses jackknifing to derive participant-level estimates that can be submitted to standard statistical tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Galle et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This method allows comparing latency differences between conditions or groups, but it is not designed to accurately estimate onsets within a single condition.
This is because the time point at which a percentage threshold is reached can be much later than the first time point at which a fixation curve exhibits the relevant change.
Moreover, the choice of percentage threshold is inherently arbitrary, with several plausible threshold values that researchers could select.
Finally, an increasingly adopted onset detection method is the bootstrap-based method proposed by Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021).
text.formatted: Finally, an increasingly adopted onset detection method is the bootstrap-based method proposed by <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref>.

text.text: This method repeatedly resamples the observed data to approximate how onset estimates would vary if the experiment were repeated.
In each iteration (2,000 in Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021), a dataset is generated by resampling with replacement within strata defined by participant, time bin, and condition.
text.formatted: In each iteration (2,000 in <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021)</ref>, a dataset is generated by resampling with replacement within strata defined by participant, time bin, and condition.

text.text: A statistical test is then applied at each time bin to evaluate the effect of interest (e.g., whether the proportion of target looks departs from chance); for computational convenience, Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) used a one-sample t-test on proportions of looks.
text.formatted: A statistical test is then applied at each time bin to evaluate the effect of interest (e.g., whether the proportion of target looks departs from chance); for computational convenience, <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref> used a one-sample t-test on proportions of looks.

text.text: An onset is defined as the first time point in a sustained 200 ms run of significant tests.
Thus, as in sequential testing approaches, the method relies on a significance-based criterion, avoiding the need to define onset via an arbitrary magnitude threshold.

Crucially, however, because the criterion is evaluated across many bootstrap resamples, the method yields a full distribution of onset estimates, which can be summarised by its mean and confidence interval (Carpenter & Bithell, 2000; DiCiccio & Efron, 1996).

text.text: This distribution quantifies the temporal uncertainty around the onset and supports comparisons of onset times between conditions or participant groups. Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) first illustrated the bootstrap-based method in a visual world experiment on predictive gender processing in first-and second-language speakers of German.

text.text: However, an important limitation of the bootstrap-based method is that its accuracy in recovering underlying onset values has not been formally assessed (but see Minor, 2026, for an evaluation of its Type I error rate when comparing latencies between groups).

text.text: Moreover, as is the case for other onset detection methods, the bootstrap-based method treats fixation curves primarily as a vehicle for extracting a single timing index, but does not model how fixation curves change over time or how different experimental manipulations shape these trajectories (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021).

text.text: This limitation is particularly salient given the field's shift toward increasingly fine-grained timecourse analyses (Ito & Knoeferle, 2023; McMurray, 2023; Porretta et al., 2018).

text.text: Researchers who wish to characterise fixation curves over time must therefore complement onset analyses with other methods such as GAMMs or growth-curve models (e.g., Ivanova-Sullivan et al., 2024; Schlenter & Westergaard, 2024).

text.text: The current article proposes a novel GAMM-based method that addresses limitations of existing approaches by integrating curve-fitting (model-based) and index-based (onset detection) approaches.
The method uses GAMMs to model the full timecourse of looking preferences and then performs onset detection on the basis of predictions from the fitted model.

Like the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021), the GAMM-based method yields a distribution of onset estimates that quantifies uncertainty around onset times and supports their comparison across experimental conditions and participant groups.
text.formatted: Like the bootstrap-based method of <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref>, the GAMM-based method yields a distribution of onset estimates that quantifies uncertainty around onset times and supports their comparison across experimental conditions and participant groups.

text.text: In the following sections, we describe the main steps of the GAMM-based onset detection method.
Next, we demonstrate its applicability by reanalysing two visual world datasets (Studies 1 and 2).

Finally, we evaluate the GAMM-based method and the bootstrapbased method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) in two simulation analyses (Study 3) and show that the GAMM-based method yields more accurate onset estimates and generally better confidence interval coverage.
text.formatted: Finally, we evaluate the GAMM-based method and the bootstrapbased method of <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref> in two simulation analyses (Study 3) and show that the GAMM-based method yields more accurate onset estimates and generally better confidence interval coverage.

text.text: The onset detection method proposed here is designed to achieve two aims: (a) estimate when an effect first emerges in visual world fixation curves, and (b) enable statistical comparisons of onset times between conditions and participant groups.
The method can estimate two different types of onsets, which we refer to as "simple onsets" and "difference curve onsets".
Simple onsets are defined within a single condition.
They capture the earliest time point at which looks to the target image show a reliable increase.

Thus, simple onsets indicate when the probability of a target (vs. non-target) look first increases (e.g., when participants begin to anticipate a target noun before it is heard, Jackson et al., 2025; Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Thus, simple onsets indicate when the probability of a target (vs. non-target) look first increases (e.g., when participants begin to anticipate a target noun before it is heard, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Jackson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Difference curve onsets are defined in terms of a between-condition contrast.
They estimate the earliest time point at which the corresponding fixation curves diverge reliably from one another.

Thus, difference curve onsets indicate when a predictor of interest first has a detectable effect on the timecourse (e.g., when participants begin to use vowel length to discriminate between two words, McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013).
text.formatted: Thus, difference curve onsets indicate when a predictor of interest first has a detectable effect on the timecourse (e.g., when participants begin to use vowel length to discriminate between two words, <ref type="bibr">McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the method supports statistical comparisons of onset timing for both onset types.

Such comparisons address the kinds of questions that often motivate onset analyses in the first place; for example, whether an effect emerges earlier or later in one condition or group than another (e.g., whether predictive looks arise earlier in first-than in secondlanguage comprehenders, Jackson et al., 2025), or whether a contrast shows an earlier onset than a second contrast (e.g., whether the effect of a formant manipulation arises earlier than that of vowel length, Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013).
text.formatted: Such comparisons address the kinds of questions that often motivate onset analyses in the first place; for example, whether an effect emerges earlier or later in one condition or group than another (e.g., whether predictive looks arise earlier in first-than in secondlanguage comprehenders, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Jackson et al., 2025)</ref>, or whether a contrast shows an earlier onset than a second contrast (e.g., whether the effect of a formant manipulation arises earlier than that of vowel length, <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In the applications below, Study 1 illustrates the estimation and comparison of simple onsets, whereas Study 2 illustrates difference curve onsets and how they can be compared.

The application of the GAMM-based method entails four main steps (see Fig. 1): (a) fitting a GAMM to model fixation curves over time; (b) simulating multiple fixation curves from the fitted model; (c) estimating an onset time for each simulated curve, yielding an onset distribution; and (d) summarising the onset distribution in terms of its central tendency and uncertainty intervals and, when relevant, comparing distributions of onset times.
text.formatted: The application of the GAMM-based method entails four main steps (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>): (a) fitting a GAMM to model fixation curves over time; (b) simulating multiple fixation curves from the fitted model; (c) estimating an onset time for each simulated curve, yielding an onset distribution; and (d) summarising the onset distribution in terms of its central tendency and uncertainty intervals and, when relevant, comparing distributions of onset times.

text.text: Before describing the steps in detail, we briefly motivate the use of GAMMs for analysing visual world data and highlight their practical advantages.
We adopted GAMMs as the statistical modelling foundation for our onset detection method because they can accommodate several characteristics of visual world eye-tracking data.
First, the dependent variable in visual world eye-tracking is binary because gaze samples can be coded as falling (or not) on a particular image of interest.
Since GAMMs are an extension of generalised linear models, they can accommodate binary responses by assuming a binomial response distribution (Barr, 2008; Jaeger, 2008).
text.formatted: Since GAMMs are an extension of generalised linear models, they can accommodate binary responses by assuming a binomial response distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Jaeger, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Second, fixation curves can display strong non-linearities over time.

For example, when participants hear an object name (e.g., beaker), looks to a phonological competitor (e.g., beetle) may initially increase, but then decrease once the target's name is fully heard (Allopenna et al., 1998; Huettig & McQueen, 2007).

text.text: Growth-curve models approximate these dynamics with polynomial terms (e.g., Mirman, 2014).
text.formatted: Growth-curve models approximate these dynamics with polynomial terms (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Mirman, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, fixation curves may show non-linearities that are difficult to model even with higher-order polynomials (e.g., an extended baseline followed by a rapid increase).

GAMMs instead represent time using smooths, non-linear functions that can flexibly accommodate a wide range of shapes without requiring the researcher to assume a particular functional form (Baayen et al., 2017; Miwa & Baayen, 2021).
text.formatted: GAMMs instead represent time using smooths, non-linear functions that can flexibly accommodate a wide range of shapes without requiring the researcher to assume a particular functional form <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Baayen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Miwa & Baayen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Third, because time bins are nested within participants, observations are not independent.
As in mixed-effects models more generally, GAMMs capture this clustering by including random intercepts and slopes (Porretta et al., 2018; Sóskuthy, 2017).
text.formatted: As in mixed-effects models more generally, GAMMs capture this clustering by including random intercepts and slopes <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Porretta et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Sóskuthy, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, visual world data exhibit strong autocorrelation because eye-trackers sample at high rates, but planning and executing a saccade takes around 200 ms (Hallett, 1986; Salverda et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Fourth, visual world data exhibit strong autocorrelation because eye-trackers sample at high rates, but planning and executing a saccade takes around 200 ms <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hallett, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Salverda et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Ignoring autocorrelation leads to underestimation of standard errors and inflation of Type I error rates (Baayen et al., 2018; Van Rij et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Ignoring autocorrelation leads to underestimation of standard errors and inflation of Type I error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Baayen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Van Rij et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: GAMMs can incorporate an AR(1) error structure that allows residuals at adjacent time points to be correlated (Wood, 2017).
text.formatted: GAMMs can incorporate an AR(1) error structure that allows residuals at adjacent time points to be correlated <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Wood, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: While this is an approximation-because the degree of autocorrelation depends on how the data are discretised over time and on the underlying fixation dynamics (McMurray, 2023)-it can nevertheless ameliorate the problem and is preferable to assuming independent errors.
In sum, visual world eye-tracking data have characteristics that are challenging for other analytical approaches but can be addressed naturally within GAMMs (e.g., Porretta et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In sum, visual world eye-tracking data have characteristics that are challenging for other analytical approaches but can be addressed naturally within GAMMs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Porretta et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: With these advantages in mind, we now turn to Step 1 and describe the data preprocessing and model specification.
Before fitting the GAMM, we process the eye-tracking data to obtain a binomial response variable for model fitting.
Gaze samples are binned into 20 ms intervals within each trial.
Each bin is then binarised by coding it as 1 if a majority of valid samples in that bin fall on the target image and as 0 otherwise.
Because binarisation produces a single data point per time bin in each trial, it effectively downsamples the data to 50 Hz (Porretta et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Because binarisation produces a single data point per time bin in each trial, it effectively downsamples the data to 50 Hz <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Porretta et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Following usage in the visual world literature (e.g., Ito & Knoeferle, 2023), we will refer to these 0/1 observations as "looks"-not "fixations"-to make clear that our dependent measure is based on eye-tracker gaze samples rather than on the detection of oculomotor events.
text.formatted: Following usage in the visual world literature (e.g., Ito & Knoeferle, 2023), we will refer to these 0/1 observations as "looks"-not "fixations"-to make clear that our dependent measure is based on eye-tracker gaze samples rather than on the detection of oculomotor events.

text.text: Note, however, that some visual world studies use the term "look" to refer to a saccade together with a subsequent fixation (e.g., McMurray et al., 2002; Rigler et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Note, however, that some visual world studies use the term "look" to refer to a saccade together with a subsequent fixation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">McMurray et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Rigler et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The definition of which observations are coded as 1 versus 0 depends on the research question of interest.
In all analyses in the current paper, one image of interest was coded as 1 and the remaining images in the display as 0; for simplicity, we refer to these as target and non-target looks.
Blinks, saccades, and looks outside the image areas were considered invalid and thus excluded.

Under this coding, a predicted target-looking probability of 50% indicates an equal probability of looking to the target and to all non-target images (taken together), whereas values greater than 50% indicate a greater probability of looking to the target than to all non-target images (taken together).
Other comparisons can be implemented through alternative binomial codings of the dependent variable.

For example, when a display contains several non-target images, a researcher interested specifically in looks to the target versus a specific competitor image would code looks to the target and competitor as 1 and 0 respectively, while excluding looks to the remaining images.
The onset detection method itself is compatible with any binomial coding that is appropriate for the research question.

After binarisation, we aggregate the trial-level 0/1 looks by summing across trials to obtain the number of trials coded as 1 (target_looks) and the number of trials contributing valid data (total_looks) for each participant × condition × bin combination.
These binomial counts (target_looks out of total_looks) constitute the GAMM's response variablefoot_0 , and are used to model how the probability of target looks changes over time.
text.formatted: These binomial counts (target_looks out of total_looks) constitute the GAMM's response variable<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> , and are used to model how the probability of target looks changes over time.

text.text: Equivalently, one can say that the GAMM models the proportion of looks to the target image (target_looks / total_looks).
However, these proportions are not precomputed for model fitting.
Rather, the model is fitted directly to the binomial counts, these counts are modelled on a latent log-odds scale, and the fixation curves are obtained as predicted probabilities from the GAMM.
We adopted these binarisation and aggregation processing steps for two main reasons.
First, they greatly reduce the size of the dataset, reducing the computational time required for model fitting and for the simulations conducted in subsequent steps.

Second, aggregating trial-level data helps reduce autocorrelation by collapsing within-trial runs of identical 0/1 observations into participant-level binomial counts, yielding a smoother and more stable timecourse of target looks.
Finally, to account for the remaining autocorrelation, we fit an autoregressive GAMM with an AR(1) term.

However, because the mgcv package requires the magnitude of autocorrelation to be supplied rather than estimated, we follow a two-step approach (Van Rij et al., 2019): we first fit a GAMM with no explicit autocorrelation structure, estimate the lag-1 residual autocorrelation from that model, and then refit the same GAMM with an AR(1) term that is fixed to the estimated value.
text.formatted: However, because the mgcv package requires the magnitude of autocorrelation to be supplied rather than estimated, we follow a two-step approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Van Rij et al., 2019)</ref>: we first fit a GAMM with no explicit autocorrelation structure, estimate the lag-1 residual autocorrelation from that model, and then refit the same GAMM with an AR(1) term that is fixed to the estimated value.

text.text: The GAMMs employed here all included by-participant random intercepts, allowing each participant to have their own overall probability of target-looking within the analysis window, and by-participant random slopes for time, allowing participant-specific deviations in the timecourse of target looks.
Additionally, each random effect was allowed to vary by condition, so that individual differences with respect to the experimental conditions could also be captured.
Our models did not include random effects for items because the response variable was aggregated across items (we return to this limitation and its implications in the General Discussion).
A binomial GAMM provides two types of results that are of interest in visual world analyses.
First, the parametric component provides estimates of overall target-looking (relative to non-target looks) in each experimental condition.
These estimates can be considered an interpretable index of the fixation curve, in the sense introduced above.
They can be used, for example, to diagnose predictive effects before the spoken presentation of a target word (e.g., Lago et al., 2023; Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021).
text.formatted: They can be used, for example, to diagnose predictive effects before the spoken presentation of a target word (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Lago et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the GAMM includes non-linear smooth terms that model how target-looking changes over time (Miwa & Baayen, 2021; Porretta et al., 2018) (see Fig. 1, panel 1), allowing researchers to test whether trajectories differ over time across conditions (e.g., Sóskuthy, 2017; Wieling, 2018).
text.formatted: Second, the GAMM includes non-linear smooth terms that model how target-looking changes over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Miwa & Baayen, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Porretta et al., 2018)</ref> (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, panel 1), allowing researchers to test whether trajectories differ over time across conditions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Sóskuthy, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Wieling, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These smooths can also be used to compute a difference curve and thereby identify time windows in which conditions differ.
However, GAMM output alone does not yield a principled temporal uncertainty interval for an onset estimate, which motivates the simulation-based procedure introduced below.
To quantify uncertainty in onset estimates, we need to account for the uncertainty in the model's predictions.
In a fitted GAMM, parameters can be treated as full distributions of plausible values, rather than as fixed point estimates (D. L. Miller, 2025; Wood, 2017).
text.formatted: In a fitted GAMM, parameters can be treated as full distributions of plausible values, rather than as fixed point estimates (D. L. <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Miller, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Wood, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We can draw values from these parameter distributions-a procedure called 'posterior simulation'-and compute, for each draw, the corresponding group-level fixation curve.
This results in the simulation of many plausible fixation curves, which, taken together, capture the range of predictions implied by the fitted model (see Fig. 1, panel 2).
text.formatted: This results in the simulation of many plausible fixation curves, which, taken together, capture the range of predictions implied by the fitted model (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, panel 2).

text.text: Each simulated curve therefore represents a plausible timecourse implied by the fitted model, given the uncertainty in the estimated parameters.

This simulation process is conceptually similar to the bootstrap method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) in that it yields a distribution of onset estimates, but variability is generated from the fitted statistical model rather than by resampling the observed data.
text.formatted: This simulation process is conceptually similar to the bootstrap method of <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref> in that it yields a distribution of onset estimates, but variability is generated from the fitted statistical model rather than by resampling the observed data.

text.text: To obtain stable results, the analyses in Studies 1 and 2 below were based on 10,000 simulated curves.
Each simulated curve is then passed to Step 3 to obtain an onset estimate.
For each simulated curve, a simple onset is defined as the earliest time point at which predicted target-looking is reliably greater than its baseline value.
Specifically, for each simulated fixation curve, we record the predicted value at the baseline time 𝑡 0 (on the modelled log-odds scale) and then traverse the curve from left to right.

At each time point 𝑡 𝑛 , we treat the baseline value 𝜂(𝑡 0 ) as a fixed reference for that simulated curve and compute a one-sided 95% confidence interval for the predicted value at 𝑡 𝑛 from the fitted GAMM.
If the lower bound of this interval at 𝑡 𝑛 exceeds 𝜂(𝑡 0 ), we record 𝑡 𝑛 as the onset (see Fig. 1, panel 3).
text.formatted: If the lower bound of this interval at 𝑡 𝑛 exceeds 𝜂(𝑡 0 ), we record 𝑡 𝑛 as the onset (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, panel 3).

text.text: The result of this process is a full distribution of onset times, one for each simulated curve.
Note that because an onset is defined relative to the baseline time, the criterion automatically corrects for baseline differences between conditions (Barr, 2008; Barr et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Note that because an onset is defined relative to the baseline time, the criterion automatically corrects for baseline differences between conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barr, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Barr et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Difference curve onsets can be obtained in the same way, but now on the basis of a contrast between two predicted fixation curves.
Specifically, for each simulation draw, we compute the predicted difference curve over time.
A difference curve onset is then defined as the earliest time point 𝑡 𝑛 at which the lower bound of a one-sided 95% interval for the difference curve exceeds its value at the baseline time 𝑡 0 .
Conceptually, this amounts to evaluating when the two trajectories begin to diverge after aligning them at baseline.
As with simple onsets, repeating this process across simulation draws yields a distribution of difference curve onsets.

We emphasise that, in our method, the criterion for onset detection is reached only when the predicted trajectory reliably exceeds the baseline value, operationalised here by the use of a one-sided confidence interval.
This kind of definition has three related advantages.
First, it anchors our onset criterion to evidential strength, because onsets are detected only when the baseline value is exceeded with enough certainty.
This helps prevent small fluctuations due to measurement noise from being treated as onsets.

Second, as is the case for sequential testing approaches (e.g., Ben-David et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2018) and for the bootstrap-based method (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021), our method does not require specifying an arbitrary magnitude threshold, thereby reducing researcher degrees of freedom associated with threshold selection.
text.formatted: Second, as is the case for sequential testing approaches (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Ben-David et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ito et al., 2018)</ref> and for the bootstrap-based method <ref type="bibr">(Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021)</ref>, our method does not require specifying an arbitrary magnitude threshold, thereby reducing researcher degrees of freedom associated with threshold selection.

text.text: Third, because the criterion is standardised (i.e., tied to the standard error on the modelled scale), it is broadly portable across tasks and designs, effects of different magnitudes, and model specifications.

By contrast, absolute magnitude thresholds and percent-of-maximum thresholds have often required study-specific criteria in different visual world studies (Galle et al., 2019; McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013).
text.formatted: By contrast, absolute magnitude thresholds and percent-of-maximum thresholds have often required study-specific criteria in different visual world studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Galle et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, a limitation of using an evidence-based criterion is that onset estimates can depend on the uncertainty around the estimated fixation curves.
For example, studies with greater uncertainty (e.g., with smaller sample sizes or greater variability) may yield later onsets, because greater uncertainty may delay when the criterion is satisfied.
For this reason, we have additionally implemented a version of the GAMM-based method that uses a magnitude threshold, in which an onset is detected when the baseline is exceeded by a fixed amount.
As a robustness check, we have additionally analysed Studies 1 and 2 with different magnitude thresholds (Appendix S1 in the Supplementary Materials).
In addition, in Study 3 we evaluate how onset estimates obtained with our default criterion depend on sample size, variability, and the shape of the underlying fixation curves.
The final step of the GAMM-based method is to summarise the onset distribution.

A point estimate can be obtained using a measure of central tendency (e.g., a mean or median), whereas the uncertainty around the estimate can be quantified using an interval derived from the onset distribution (see Fig. 1, panel 4).
text.formatted: A point estimate can be obtained using a measure of central tendency (e.g., a mean or median), whereas the uncertainty around the estimate can be quantified using an interval derived from the onset distribution (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, panel 4).

text.text: Because onset distributions can be skewed or otherwise asymmetric, we recommend reporting medians and highest-density intervals (HDIs).

A 95% HDI is the smallest contiguous region containing 95% of the distribution's mass and is less sensitive to outliers than standard quantile-based intervals (Hyndman, 1996; Kruschke & Liddell, 2018).
text.formatted: A 95% HDI is the smallest contiguous region containing 95% of the distribution's mass and is less sensitive to outliers than standard quantile-based intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hyndman, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kruschke & Liddell, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Once we obtain full distributions of onset estimates (for either simple onsets or difference curve onsets), onset times can be directly compared between conditions or groups.

Specifically, for any contrast of interest, we take the onset estimate from each simulation draw in one condition or group and subtract the corresponding onset estimate from the same draw in the other condition or group.
This process yields a paired distribution of onset differences.
Summarising this distribution by its median and 95% HDI quantifies the comparison and its uncertainty.
If the 95% HDI excludes zero, this provides evidence that the two onsets differ in timing.
Having outlined the four steps, we now turn to empirical applications.
In Study 1, we apply the method to an existing visual world experiment to illustrate the estimation and comparison of simple onsets between two experimental conditions.

text.text: This study applies the GAMM-based method to a visual world eye-tracking experiment reported by Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021).
text.formatted: This study applies the GAMM-based method to a visual world eye-tracking experiment reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: The authors tested the processing of German possessive pronouns, which encode both prospective (forward-looking) and retrospective (backward-looking) gender agreement dependencies.
The suffix of the possessive pronoun encodes a prospective dependency, because it agrees in gender with a subsequent noun (the possessee).
Meanwhile, the stem of the pronoun encodes a retrospective dependency, because it agrees in gender with a preceding antecedent noun (the possessor).

For example, in Sarah fem verliert ihr fem -en masc Knopf masc 'Sarah loses her button', the pronoun ihren 'her' agrees in gender with both Knopf 'button' (the possessee) and Sarah (the antecedent or possessor).

In two visual world eye-tracking experiments, German-speaking participants heard spoken instructions such as 'Click on her blue button!', while looking at a display showing a target object (e.g., a blue button masc ) and a competitor object, with the same colour as the target object but a different grammatical gender (e.g., a blue bottle fem ).
The pronoun's stem agreed in gender with the antecedent, but either matched (sein masc -en masc Knopf masc 'his button') or mismatched (ihr fem -en masc Knopf masc 'her button') the suffix's gender.
Crucially, the gender of the suffix could be used to predict the identity of the target noun in both conditions.
The conditions only differed in the information expressed by the pronoun stem, which was not syntactically informative for predicting the target.

The key research question was whether the pronoun stem, despite being irrelevant for prediction, would nonetheless interfere with the prediction process, thus causing a processing delay in the mismatch versus match condition.

Here we focus on Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021) Experiment 2 (a higher-powered replication of their Experiment 1), which tested 74 German speakers on 96 target-competitor image pairs (each participant saw 48 trials in each condition).
text.formatted: Here we focus on <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021)</ref> Experiment 2 (a higher-powered replication of their Experiment 1), which tested 74 German speakers on 96 target-competitor image pairs (each participant saw 48 trials in each condition).

text.text: Stone, Veríssimo, et al. reported two analyses: a "window analysis" of proportions of looks over the whole predictive time window (from the beginning of the pronoun until the beginning of the target noun in the spoken instruction), and an onset analysis using the bootstrap-based method.

The window analysis revealed that participants looked predictively at the target object in both experimental conditions, but that the predictive effect was larger in the match than in the mismatch condition.
The onset analysis showed that the predictive effect started significantly earlier in the match than in the mismatch condition (mean onsets of 402 ms vs. 709 ms).
Thus, the results indicated that the timecourse of predictions was influenced by the (syntactically irrelevant) antecedent agreement dependency.
We have reanalysed Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021) dataset with the GAMM-based method proposed here.
text.formatted: We have reanalysed <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021)</ref> dataset with the GAMM-based method proposed here.

text.text: We present three complementary types of results, all of which can be obtained from the same fitted model: (a) a comparison of overall proportions of target looks in the two conditions, which is akin to the window analysis reported by Stone, Veríssimo, et al.; (b) a timecourse analysis of how the fixation curves in the two conditions differ over time; and (c) an onset analysis that produces estimates of the onsets of predictive effects and their comparison between conditions.
text.formatted: We present three complementary types of results, all of which can be obtained from the same fitted model: (a) a comparison of overall proportions of target looks in the two conditions, which is akin to the window analysis reported by <ref type="bibr">Stone, Veríssimo, et al.; (b)</ref> a timecourse analysis of how the fixation curves in the two conditions differ over time; and (c) an onset analysis that produces estimates of the onsets of predictive effects and their comparison between conditions.

As in Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), all analyses were conducted on a predictive window that extended from the beginning of the possessive pronoun to the beginning of the target noun plus 200 ms (to account for the time taken to programme a saccade, Hallett, 1986; Salverda et al., 2014).

text.text: The GAMMs included a fixed effect of condition (sum-coded; match = -0.5; mismatch = 0.5), and a non-linear time smooth for each level of condition.
Each smooth used the default basis dimension in mgcv (k = 10).
Note that the choice of contrasts affects only the parametric part of the GAMM, which summarises overall target-looking across the analysis window (on the modelled log-odds scale).

By contrast, the non-linear smooths are insensitive to the contrast coding of the condition fixed effect; instead, the timecourse of looks is captured by condition-specific smooths (one per condition level).
To obtain a direct inferential test of match versus mismatch timecourse differences, we additionally fitted a re-parameterised GAMM with condition coded as an ordered factor.

With this parameterisation, the match condition serves as the reference smooth and the additional smooth represents the difference in timecourse between the mismatch and match conditions, yielding a p-value for this difference smooth (Wood, 2017; see also Sóskuthy, 2017; Wieling, 2018).

text.text: We first fitted a non-autoregressive GAMM, which displayed a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of r = 0.89; we then refitted the model with an AR(1) error structure using this value.
The parametric part of the model, analogous to intercepts and slopes in a linear regression model, showed a significant intercept term (b = 0.95; z = 28.83; p < .001).
text.formatted: The parametric part of the model, analogous to intercepts and slopes in a linear regression model, showed a significant intercept term (b = 0.95; z = 28.83; p < .001).

text.text: Because condition was sum-coded, the parametric intercept corresponds to the mean log-odds of target (vs. competitor) looks across the match and mismatch conditions.

This result indicates that comprehenders looked more to the target than to the competitor during the analysis window, suggesting that the target was predicted prior to being heard in the spoken instruction.

The condition slope-which reflects the difference between conditions in the target-over-competitor advantage-was negative, reflecting a smaller target advantage in the mismatch condition, but this difference was not statistically significant (b = -0.09; z = -1.30; p = .195).

Accordingly, the significant smooths indicate that target-over-competitor looks changed over time in both conditions, with the large effective degrees of freedom suggesting markedly non-linear timecourses.

text.text: Temporal onsets.
Predictive effects were estimated to begin at 317 [146, 545] ms in the match condition and at 671 [609, 721] ms in the mismatch condition (see Fig. 2B for the full distributions of onsets).
text.formatted: Predictive effects were estimated to begin at 317 <ref type="bibr">[146,</ref> <ref type="bibr">545]</ref> ms in the match condition and at 671 <ref type="bibr">[609,</ref> <ref type="bibr">721]</ref> ms in the mismatch condition (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref> for the full distributions of onsets).

text.text: These estimates correspond to simple onsets, defined within each condition.

To compare onset times between conditions, we obtained a distribution of onset differences by subtracting, for each simulation draw, the onset in the match condition from the corresponding onset in the mismatch condition.

The comparison showed that the mismatch condition had a significantly later onset than the match condition (351 [87, 545] ms), consistent with the bootstrap-based results of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021).

text.text: As a robustness check, we repeated the onset estimation and between-condition comparison using four magnitude thresholds (0, 0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 log-odds; Appendix S1 in the target noun Supplementary Materials).

Onsets were estimated to occur later as the magnitude threshold increased, but generally yielded the same conclusion as the default evidence-based criterion, with an earlier onset in the match than in the mismatch condition.

To illustrate this, we ran an analysis in which an onset was defined as the first time point with a reliably smaller proportion of target-versus-competitor looks than at the baseline time.

text.text: Both the GAMM-based method proposed here and the bootstrap-based method showed that comprehenders predicted the target noun, and that this prediction had a distinct timecourse in the match versus mismatch conditions.

Specifically, predictive effects arose earlier when the gender of the pronoun stem (which agrees with the possessor/antecedent) matched the gender of the target object, as compared to when it mismatched.

As discussed by Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), this suggests that the computation of coreference between the pronoun and its antecedent interfered with the prediction process, showing an interaction between antecedent retrieval and predictive processes.

This difference likely stems from the different statistical models that were fitted. Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021) employed a generalised mixed-effects model that did not include time as a predictor.

text.text: In contrast, our GAMM analysis modelled fixation curves over time, with the model's parametric terms summarising overall target-looking across the whole analysis window.
In this respect, the GAMM-based method provides a more comprehensive analysis, because it jointly characterises curve shape and derives onset times within a single model.

Another discrepancy between our results and those of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021) was that the GAMM-based onset detection method produced earlier onset estimates than those of the bootstrap-based method (GAMM-based method: 317 ms and 671 ms for the match and mismatch conditions; bootstrap-based method: 402 ms and 709 ms).

(2021)</ref> was that the GAMM-based onset detection method produced earlier onset estimates than those of the bootstrap-based method (GAMM-based method: 317 ms and 671 ms for the match and mismatch conditions; bootstrap-based method: 402 ms and 709 ms).

text.text: Moreover, the 95% intervals produced by the bootstrap-based method were narrower than those from the GAMM-based method, in the match condition (95% interval width of GAMMbased method: 399 ms; bootstrap-based method: 83 ms), the mismatch condition (112 ms vs. 34 ms) and their difference (458 ms vs. 90 ms).
Clearly, the two onset detection methods can yield different answers with regard to the timing and uncertainty of the estimated onsets.
The GAMM-based method's ability to detect earlier effects suggests that it may have greater temporal sensitivity than the bootstrap-based method.
Moreover, the fact that the bootstrap-based method produced narrower intervals suggests that it might underestimate the uncertainty around onsets.
Before turning to a formal evaluation of the two methods (Study 3), we next apply the GAMM-based method to a second dataset that illustrates the estimation and comparison of difference curve onsets.

In the previous section, the GAMM-based method was applied to an experimental design in which the central research question concerned estimating and comparing simple onsets, defined within each condition as the onset of a target-over-competitor advantage.

In many cases, however, the key question cannot be answered by examining when a preference emerges within a single condition, but instead requires comparing fixation curves across conditions to determine when a predictor first has a detectable effect on the timecourse.
In such situations, the relevant quantity is a difference curve onset, defined as the earliest time point at which the fixation curves in two different conditions begin to diverge.

A case in point is "target-absent designs", in which target and competitor objects do not co-exist within the same visual display (i.e., they are not presented within the same trial), but instead belong to different within-participant conditions.

An example is a visual world study by Ito et al. (2018), which investigated the activation of target words and phonological competitors in L1 English speakers and L1 Japanese-L2 English speakers (for other examples of target-absent designs, see Huettig & Altmann, 2005; Rommers et al., 2013).
text.formatted: An example is a visual world study by <ref type="bibr">Ito et al. (2018)</ref>, which investigated the activation of target words and phonological competitors in L1 English speakers and L1 Japanese-L2 English speakers (for other examples of target-absent designs, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Huettig & Altmann, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Rommers et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were presented with auditory sentences that contained a highly predictable word, such as cloud in The tourists expected rain when the sun went behind the cloud.
In each trial, participants saw a four-object visual display, which appeared 1000 ms before the presentation of the target word.
One of the four objects was the critical object.

Depending on the experimental condition, the critical object was either the target word (an image of a cloud), a phonological competitor in English (an image of a clown, which shares its initial phonemes with cloud), a phonological competitor in Japanese (an image of a bear, because the Japanese word kuma 'bear' shares its first mora with kumo 'cloud'), or an unrelated image whose name did not share any phonological or semantic features with the target word (a globe).
Only the critical object differed according to the experimental condition; the other three objects in the display (called "distractors") were held constant.

Henceforth, we use the terms "target object", "English competitor", "Japanese competitor", and "unrelated object" to refer to the critical object shown in each condition, even though these objects were not presented together in the same display.

In such a design, the effects of interest are between-condition contrasts comparing looks to the target object, the English competitor, and the Japanese competitor against looks to the unrelated object.
If participants pre-activated the target word cloud while hearing the sentence, we would expect more looks to the target object (the cloud) than to the unrelated object (the globe).
Likewise, if participants pre-activated the phonological neighbours of the target, we would expect increased looks to the English competitor (the clown) relative to the unrelated object.

For the L1 English group, the Japanese competitor served as a control: it was included to test phonological pre-activation in the L1 Japanese-L2 English group, but because the L1 participants did not speak Japanese, looks in this condition were expected to be similar to those in the unrelated condition.

We reanalysed the data from Ito et al.'s (2018) L1 group, which comprised 24 native English speakers who heard 16 experimental sentences (4 in each condition). Ito et al. (2018) analysed these data using growth-curve regression models and a sequential mixed-effects analysis in 50 ms bins.

(2018)</ref> analysed these data using growth-curve regression models and a sequential mixed-effects analysis in 50 ms bins.

text.text: The sequential analysis showed that participants were more likely to look at the target object than at the unrelated object starting 400 ms after display onset.
In addition, participants were more likely to look at the English competitor than at the unrelated object, but this effect was limited to a narrower time window between 500 and 650 ms.
Ito and Knoeferle (2023) subsequently reanalysed this dataset using the bootstrap-based onset detection method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021).
text.formatted: Ito and Knoeferle (2023) subsequently reanalysed this dataset using the bootstrap-based onset detection method of <ref type="bibr">Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Looks to the English competitor were not analysed with the bootstrap-based method, perhaps because this effect was confined to a relatively narrow time window in the original sequential analysis.

We applied the GAMM-based method to this dataset to obtain three complementary results: (a) a comparison of overall proportions of looks across conditions, (b) a timecourse analysis of fixation curves in each condition, and (c) estimates of difference curve onsets.
Following Ito and Knoeferle (2023), we analysed a time window that ranged from 200 ms after display onset (i.e., 800 ms before target-word onset) until 1000 ms after target-word onset.
The initial 200 ms were excluded because the data contained very few valid observations.

The dependent variable consisted of binomial counts of looks to the critical object (vs. looks to the three distractor objects in the display), aggregated for each participant × condition × 20 ms bin.

The GAMMs included a fixed effect of experimental condition (i.e., the identity of the critical object shown on a given trial) as a four-level, treatment-coded factor, with the unrelated condition as the reference level.
Thus, in the parametric part of the model, the target object, English competitor, and Japanese competitor were each compared to the unrelated condition.
The models additionally included a non-linear time smooth for each level of condition, each with the default basis dimension in mgcv (k = 10).
As in Study 1, we fitted an additional GAMM with condition coded as an ordered factor to test timecourse differences relative to the unrelated condition.

As for the random-effects structure, models included random intercepts for participants and random slopes for condition, time, and their interaction, which were justified by significantly lower fREML scores (condition: χ 2 (3) = 773.67; p < .001; time: χ 2 (1) = 515.37; p < .001; condition-varying time slopes: χ 2 (3) = 1163.67; p < .001).
text.formatted: As for the random-effects structure, models included random intercepts for participants and random slopes for condition, time, and their interaction, which were justified by significantly lower fREML scores (condition: χ 2 (3) = 773.67; p < .001; time: χ 2 (1) = 515.37; p < .001; condition-varying time slopes: χ 2 (3) = 1163.67; p < .001).

text.text: We first fitted a non-autoregressive GAMM, which displayed a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of r = 0.87; we then refitted the model with an AR(1) error structure using this value.
Overall proportions.

The GAMM's parametric terms showed that participants looked more to the target object than to the unrelated object (b = 1.56; z = 7.68; p < .001) (condition was treatment-coded with the unrelated condition as the reference level, so the condition coefficients reflect differences relative to the unrelated object).
text.formatted: The GAMM's parametric terms showed that participants looked more to the target object than to the unrelated object (b = 1.56; z = 7.68; p < .001) (condition was treatment-coded with the unrelated condition as the reference level, so the condition coefficients reflect differences relative to the unrelated object).

text.text: Looks to the English competitor were also more frequent than looks to the unrelated object, but this difference was not statistically significant (b = 0.27; z = 1.57; p = .115).
By contrast, looks to the Japanese competitor were very similar to those to the unrelated object (b = -0.01; z = -0.06; p = .951).

Note that these estimates summarise differences in target looking over the full analysis window on the modelled log-odds scale, including the 1000 ms period following the beginning of the target word.
As a result, the greater proportion of looks to the target object reflects not only its predictive activation, but also the subsequent increase in looks after the target word is heard.
To isolate predictive effects more specifically, the model would need to be fitted to a shorter window restricted to the 800 ms before the target word.
Timecourse of looking preferences.
Table 2 summarises the model's smooth terms.

text.text: The time smooths for the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions were not statistically significant, providing no evidence that looks changed systematically over the analysis window in these conditions.

By contrast, the time smooths for the target and English competitor conditions were significant, indicating that looks changed over time in these conditions (with their effective degrees of freedom indicating departures from linearity).
The fixation curves predicted by the model are displayed in Figure 3A.
text.formatted: The fixation curves predicted by the model are displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with the results for the smooth terms, the fixation curves in the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions were relatively constant over time.
Looks to the target object increased early and continued to rise during the predictive window (200-1000 ms), reaching 50-60% after the target word was heard.

Finally, the fixation curves for the English competitor increased during the predictive window (until about 600 ms), but then decreased to values similar to those in the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions.

In the ordered factor model, the difference smooth for the target condition was statistically significant (χ 2 (3.56) = 14.97; p = .004), indicating that its timecourse differed from that of the unrelated condition.
By contrast, the difference smooths for the English competitor (χ 2 (1.00) = 0.88; p = .348) and Japanese competitor conditions (χ 2 (1.00) = 0.00; p = .992) were not statistically significant.
Temporal onsets.

The temporal onsets of interest were defined as the earliest point at which the GAMM-predicted fixation curves in the target, English competitor, and Japanese competitor conditions diverged from the fixation curve in the unrelated condition.
To estimate difference curve onsets, we simulated difference curves directly from the fitted model (on the modelled log-odds scale), for each condition-minus-unrelated contrast.

Onsets were then obtained from each simulated difference curve using the same baseline-corrected criterion as in Study 1: the first time point at which the difference between conditions was reliably greater than its predicted value at the baseline time (here, 200 ms after display onset).
Figure 3B shows the distributions of difference curve onsets for the target minus unrelated contrast (left panel) and the English competitor minus unrelated contrast (middle panel).

text.text: Looks to the English competitor diverged from the unrelated image slightly later, at 342 [273, 490] ms.

Because both 95% HDIs were fully within the predictive window, the onset estimates suggest that activation of the target word (e.g., cloud) and of the phonological competitor (e.g., clown) occurred before the presentation of the target noun.

The difference curve onsets for the target and English competitor contrasts (each relative to the unrelated condition) were directly compared by subtracting paired onset times across simulation draws (Fig. 3B, right panel).
